content.title: Command-And- Control Instruments
content.intro: M5: Energy Governance for a Just Energy Transition

content.text: Regulations form the backbone of the energy transition by setting clear rules that shape how energy is produced, distributed, and consumed. This lesson explores command-and-control instruments which set enforceable targets to drive clean energy adoption. While these tools ensure compliance, modern designs increasingly combine strict mandates with market flexibility to encourage innovation. Through global examples like South Korea, Pakistan, and Barbados, we examine how well-designed regulations can deliver climate goals, economic benefits, and <ai prompt="Clarify energy justice.">energy justice 💬️</ai>, especially in developing contexts where policy clarity and institutional capacity are vital.

Regulatory instruments are fundamental tools to guide and shape energy production, distribution, and consumption. Among these, command-and-control mechanisms stand out as a traditional yet evolving approach due to the direct governmental mandates and enforcement. These regulations establish specific requirements, set limits, or dictate the adoption of certain technologies, compelling actors within the energy sector to align with policy objectives.
Historically, command-and-control regulations have proven highly effective in addressing significant environmental challenges and provides a clear framework for compliance and accountability. These regulations, typically involve three core elements: identifying environmentally harmful activities, imposing specific conditions or standards on these activities, and prohibiting non-compliant actions.
However, the application of command-and-control mechanisms is not without its complexities and limitations. A primary observation is that these regulations often provide no inherent incentive for entities to exceed the set limits once compliance is achieved. Furthermore, they can be inflexible, potentially imposing uniform standards or technologies that may not be optimally suited for all contexts or may stifle innovation. The design and implementation of such regulations can also be influenced by political processes, sometimes leading to the inclusion of loopholes or exceptions

Despite these considerations, the pivotal role of regulation in driving energy transitions remains undeniable. Regulations are instrumental in creating the necessary framework to balance competing interests, such as economic efficiency, environmental protection, and social justice within the energy sector. Without clear and effective regulatory oversight, energy markets 💬️ risk becoming chaotic and inequitable, potentially allowing private entities to prioritize profit over expanding access to underserved communities, or to disregard environmental standards in the pursuit of cheaper energy, leaving consumers vulnerable to unreliable service or price manipulation.
These instruments are categorized broadly into regulatory, economic, and informational tools, with regulatory instruments directly involving the use of rules and standards to promote sustainable energy development

content.intro: M5: Energy Governance for a Just Energy Transition
content.title: A: Performance-Based Standards Frameworks

content.text: Performance-based standards are regulatory frameworks that mandate a specific outcome , such as reducing emissions or improving <ai prompt="What is energy efficiency?">energy efficiency 💬️</ai> , without dictating the method by which that outcome must be achieved. These standards set quantitative targets (like a maximum level of CO₂ emissions per kilowatt-hour of electricity produced), but allow regulated entities the flexibility to choose how they comply. For example, a power plant may decide to switch fuels, install carbon capture technology, or upgrade turbines, as long as it meets the required emissions limit. This framework is widely used in energy governance because it promotes innovation and cost-effectiveness, while still achieving environmental or efficiency goals. Governments often apply performance standards to vehicles (e.g., fuel economy mandates), buildings (e.g., energy intensity limits), and utilities (e.g., mandated annual energy savings targets)

content.title: CO2 Emission Limits
content.body: CO2 emission limits set a maximum allowable quantity of pollutants or greenhouse gases per unit of output (e.g., gCO₂/kWh for power plants). These are widely used in power generation and industry. These limits are a critical component of environmental regulation, directly targeting the reduction of greenhouse gases from sources such as fossil fuel combustion and cement manufacturing. These limits aim to curb a country's contribution to global CO2 levels and climate change.

content.title: Energy Efficiency Standards
content.body: Energy efficiency standards are regulatory policy instruments that mandate specific levels of energy performance for products, buildings, or vehicles, aiming to reduce overall energy consumption and associated emissions. These standards are effective in driving investment in renewable energy and reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

content.title: Building Energy Intensity Ceilings/Codes
content.body: Building Energy Efficiency Codes (BEECs), also known as minimum energy performance standards (MEPS), establish an upper limit for allowed energy consumption in buildings. They are crucial for new constructions and major retrofits, aiming to exclude inefficient designs and technologies from the market and accelerate market transformation in the building sector. Regular updates to these standards are necessary to keep pace with technological advancements.

content.title: Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS)
content.body:
Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS) require electricity utilities to source a specified percentage of the electricity they sell from eligible renewable resources, which typically include wind, solar, biomass, geothermal, and certain hydroelectric facilities, depending on the jurisdiction.
To qualify as a RPS, a policy should include several key elements: a clear capacity target (defined as a percentage of total grid supply, a specified megawatt capacity, or a certain volume of energy generated in MWh), a deadline for meeting this target, a list of eligible renewable technologies (with clarification on whether existing or only new installations qualify), rules on renewable energy imports and credit trading, and an enforcement mechanism.

Although these components form the core structure, RPS designs vary significantly across countries. Their formulation often involves capacity assessments (such as solar irradiance potential), stakeholder engagement, mechanisms to stimulate renewable procurement, and safeguards to manage costs.
While RPS is a command-and-control policy in that it imposes a binding obligation, it also acts as a market enabler by allowing flexible, market-based compliance. Most RPS schemes incorporate market mechanisms such as:
Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs): tradable instruments that certify 1 MWh of electricity was generated from a renewable source. Utilities can purchase or generate RECs to meet their targets.
Carve-outs: sub-targets within the RPS that require a portion of the mandate to come from specific technologies (e.g., rooftop solar or offshore wind).
Credit multipliers: policies that increase the compliance value of RECs generated from favored technologies, effectively rewarding them more per unit of generation.

content.intro: M5: Energy Governance for a Just Energy Transition
content.title: B: Technology or Design Standards Frameworks

content.text:
Regulatory command:
“You must use this type of technology or meet this physical design spec.”

Technology or design standards are more prescriptive then the performance based instruments. They specify exactly what technologies or technical specifications must be used to comply with the regulation. Rather than targeting an outcome, this framework mandates the use of particular devices, materials, or system designs known to produce the desired effect. For instance, building energy codes may require that all new buildings be constructed with specific insulation materials, double-glazed windows, or solar water heating systems. Similarly, appliance efficiency regulations may require that all refrigerators sold meet a minimum energy performance threshold, measured in kilowatt-hours per year. These standards ensure reliability and immediate impact, especially where market failures prevent voluntary adoption of efficient technologies. However, they can be inflexible, sometimes locking out newer innovations or increasing compliance costs for those unable to meet exact technical criteria.

content.title: Mandatory Solar Thermal or PV Requirements for Buildings
content.body: Governments around the world are increasingly integrating solar energy requirements into national and subnational building codes. These mandates typically require new buildings to install solar thermal or photovoltaic (PV) systems as part of their energy compliance obligations. For example, the European Union has set phased targets for solar installations on new buildings by 2029–2030. France now requires commercial buildings and large parking lots to be partially covered with solar panels or green roofs. In Tokyo, new detached houses and low-rise apartment buildings must include solar systems. In India, while national codes like the Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC) provide the framework, cities like Lucknow have begun to implement their own rooftop solar mandates. These policies not only reduce electricity demand from the grid but also support long-term climate targets by embedding renewable energy directly into urban design.

content.title: Local Content Requirements (LCRs) in Clean Energy Technologies
content.body: LCRs are regulatory tools that mandate a minimum share of domestically produced materials, components, or labor in clean energy projects. While not always linked to specific technologies, LCRs often coexist with or reinforce technology mandates, especially in solar and wind projects.

content.title: Minimum Energy Performance Standards (MEPS) for Appliances
content.body:
MEPS are legally enforced minimum efficiency levels for appliances and equipment. They are designed to eliminate inefficient products from the market, reduce energy use, and curb emissions. MEPS are one of the most widely used design standards globally, with over 110 countries implementing them for key appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, and lighting. For instance, Ghana has banned used refrigerator imports and expanded its MEPS and labeling program to 17 additional appliances.
MEPS can also stimulate technology transfer, investment in local production, and improvements in manufacturing quality. However, it must pair them with technical assistance, human capacity building, and institutional support.

content.text: Proponents argue that LCRs promote job creation, protect emerging industries, and strengthen domestic value chains. Countries like Nigeria are supporting local solar panel manufacturing (e.g., LPV Technologies) to reduce reliance on imports, manage currency fluctuations, and increase technology access. However, critics note that poorly designed LCRs can lead to higher project costs, reduced quality, and trade distortions , especially when local manufacturing capacity is underdeveloped and therefore LCRs work best when aligned with existing industrial strengths.

content.intro: M5: Energy Governance for a Just Energy Transition
content.title: C: Prohibitive and Restrictive Frameworks

content.text: Prohibitions and restrictions are regulatory frameworks that explicitly ban the production, sale, or use of certain technologies, fuels, or practices. This approach is typically used when a particular activity or product is deemed too harmful to allow its continued operation, or when its continued use would undermine national or international climate goals. For example, many countries have introduced bans on the sale of incandescent light bulbs, given their inefficiency and the availability of better alternatives like LEDs. Some jurisdictions have set timelines for phasing out internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles, or prohibiting the construction of new coal-fired power plants after a certain year. These frameworks are highly effective in eliminating lock-in to harmful technologies but must be accompanied by support mechanisms , such as transition funds or retraining programs , to minimize economic and social disruption.

content.title: Ban on New Coal-Fired Power Plants
content.body: Phasing out coal is critical for limiting global temperature rise to 1.5°C. While coal still supplies over a third of global electricity, new plant construction must stop, and existing fleets must retire early , particularly in China, India, and Southeast Asia. However, in many developing countries, coal plants are young, subsidized, and linked to jobs, making phase-out politically and economically difficult. Just Energy Transition Partnerships (JET-Ps) in South Africa, Indonesia, and Viet Nam offer a model for managing this transition through concessional financing. Studies in China show that while coal phase-out can reduce income, it improves subjective well-being due to cleaner air and health benefits , especially when paired with clean energy job creation.

content.title: Fossil Fuel Vehicle Sales Ban
content.body: A fossil fuel vehicle sales ban prohibits the sale or import of internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles, aiming to accelerate electric vehicle (EV) adoption. For example, in 2024, Ethiopia became the first country to ban non-electric vehicle imports due to its reliance on expensive fuel imports. The ban is supported by tax incentives and foreign partnerships for local EV assembly, but faces challenges: limited grid access, high EV costs, poor rural financing, and lack of skilled mechanics. Success will depend on major investments in charging infrastructure, public awareness, and human capital , particularly in underserved regions.

content.title: Phase-Out of Inefficient Lighting (e.g., Incandescent Bulbs)
content.body:
The global phase-out of incandescent bulbs is one of the simplest and most cost-effective ways to cut emissions and energy use. Lighting accounts for nearly 20% of global electricity demand and 6% of CO₂ emissions.
Countries like the Philippines , India, South Africa, and China have distributed compact fluorescent lamps (CFLs) and transitioned to LEDs. Benefits include:
Up to 80% lower household lighting costs
Reduced national grid demand (e.g., 2,000 MW saved in the Philippines)
Avoided need for new power plants
Creation of green jobs and $100+ billion in annual global savings
Despite challenges like upfront bulb costs, support from international finance and development partners has made rapid implementation possible , especially where governments distribute efficient lighting at scale.

content.intro: M5: Energy Governance for a Just Energy Transition
content.title: D: Permitting, Licensing, and Siting Regulations

content.text: Permitting, licensing, and siting regulations govern the legal approval process for building and operating energy infrastructure. These frameworks determine where, how, and under what conditions projects such as power plants, transmission lines, or renewable energy installations can be developed. A developer might need to apply for a license to generate electricity, a permit to access the grid, and land-use approval from local authorities , all within a legally defined process. In many countries, <ai prompt="Tell me more about environmental impact assessments.">environmental impact assessments 💬️</ai> (EIAs) are a mandatory prerequisite for energy projects, ensuring that social and ecological concerns are addressed before construction begins. Additionally, zoning laws may restrict the siting of wind farms near residential areas or environmentally sensitive zones. These frameworks are critical for ensuring that energy infrastructure is aligned with safety, environmental, and community standards, though they can also become bottlenecks if not streamlined or transparent.

content.title: Generation Licenses
content.body: Generation licenses are formal approvals required for the construction and operation of power generation facilities. These licenses typically vary by technology (e.g., solar, wind, thermal), ownership (public utility or independent power producer), and capacity thresholds. Many jurisdictions implement tiered systems,for example, requiring full licenses for large-scale projects while allowing simplified registrations or exemptions for systems under a certain kilowatt threshold. The aim is to ensure that generators meet technical, financial, and operational criteria aligned with national energy planning, reliability, and environmental goals.

content.title: Fossil Fuel Vehicle Sales Ban
content.body: A fossil fuel vehicle sales ban prohibits the sale or import of internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles, aiming to accelerate electric vehicle (EV) adoption. For example, in 2024, Ethiopia became the first country to ban non-electric vehicle imports due to its reliance on expensive fuel imports. The ban is supported by tax incentives and foreign partnerships for local EV assembly, but faces challenges: limited grid access, high EV costs, poor rural financing, and lack of skilled mechanics. Success will depend on major investments in charging infrastructure, public awareness, and human capital , particularly in underserved regions.

content.title: Land-use Zoning for Wind and Solar Farms
content.body:
Land-use zoning regulations dictate the spatial allocation of energy infrastructure. These regulations can designate specific areas for renewable energy development, such as wind or solar farms, or conversely, restrict such development in environmentally sensitive or densely populated regions. The purpose is to manage the physical footprint of energy projects and mitigate potential conflicts with other land uses.
The development of utility-scale wind and solar farms necessitates significant land areas. For instance, a solar farm may require five to seven acres per megawatt of productive capacity, often involving extensive land grading and vegetation clearing. This substantial land demand creates inherent tension in regions already contending with competing land uses, particularly in developing countries. Global projections indicate a need for agricultural land to increase significantly by 2050 to meet rising food demand, intensifying the scarcity of available land for renewable energy projects. This competition underscores the complex challenge of balancing food security with energy transition goals.

content.text:
Furthermore, renewable energy facilities frequently overlap with important conservation areas, leading to considerable local impacts on biodiversity. Wind turbines, for example, can affect volant species, while solar photovoltaic (PV) installations can result in vegetation removal and soil degradation. The conversion of agricultural land for large-scale solar projects can displace cropland or disrupt vital irrigation infrastructure, raising concerns about long-term food production capacity, even if leasing land offers supplemental income to farmers.
A particularly sensitive aspect in developing nations involves land use conflicts with Indigenous territories. Many renewable energy projects, such as those in the Thar Desert in India, are sited on lands traditionally used by local communities for their livelihoods, sustenance, and cultural identity. The acquisition of these community-protected lands, known as 'Orans' in India, often occurs without adequate consultation or effective impact assessments, leading to human rights violations and economic disruption for Indigenous communities. This lack of Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC) in some cases creates significant opposition and can stall project development.

The interconnectedness of land use, social equity, and project viability is a profound challenge. The sheer spatial requirements of renewable energy projects inevitably create friction with existing land uses, especially in land-constrained developing countries. When land allocation processes lack transparency and inclusive dialogue, or fail to secure the consent of affected Indigenous Peoples, the resulting social conflicts can become major impediments to achieving renewable energy policy objectives. This demonstrates that the success of land-use regulations hinges not only on technical and environmental considerations but also, crucially, on robust social impact assessments, genuine community engagement, and equitable compensation mechanisms. Without addressing these social dimensions, C&C measures, no matter how well-intentioned, risk undermining the very sustainability goals they aim to achieve, transforming potential progress into public opposition and project delays. This complex interplay necessitates an integrated approach to land use in energy planning that prioritizes social justice alongside environmental and economic objectives

content.intro: M5: Energy Governance for a Just Energy Transition
content.title: E: Operational and Dispatch Regulations

content.text:
Regulatory Command:
“This is how you must behave once you’re in the system.”

Operational and market access regulations control how actors behave once they are inside the energy system. These frameworks dictate the rules of participation, such as who gets access to the grid, how electricity is dispatched, or under what technical standards generators must operate. For example, many countries have implemented priority dispatch rules for renewable energy, meaning that wind or solar electricity must be used first before fossil-based electricity can enter the grid. Others impose curtailment rules during periods of oversupply or grid congestion. Grid codes are another essential part of this framework, ensuring that all connected generators maintain voltage, frequency, and stability standards to keep the system reliable. These regulations help balance competition, security, and environmental goals in real time , and they are particularly important as energy systems become more decentralized and variable with the rise of renewables.

content.title: Grid Connection Permissions
content.body: These permissions regulate how small-scale and distributed generators,like rooftop solar or mini-grids,are formally integrated into the national grid. They require formal agreements covering safety, technical compliance, and tariff terms. Inconsistent or opaque standards often impede distributed generation (DG), creating barriers to decentralized renewable energy deployment. A study covering the Organization of Eastern Caribbean States highlights how equitable DG access relies heavily on streamlined, transparent interconnection guidelines and shared infrastructure capacity . Kenya’s Energy Act 2019, for instance, has enhanced rooftop solar deployment by setting clear connection requirements and simplifying permissions.

content.title: Interconnection Codes & Technical Standards
content.body: This subcategory includes engineering and safety rules ensuring distributed energy systems can operate without compromising grid reliability. These codes address aspects like voltage, frequency, anti-islanding protections, and protective relays. Globally, IEEE 1547 is widely adopted as the benchmark for DER interconnection . Without such standards, grids may face synchronization issues, voltage instability, or power quality problems when integrating distributed renewables.

content.title: Metering Requirements
content.body: Metering regulations define how electricity generation and consumption are recorded, and it is crucial for compensation under schemes like net metering, feed-in tariffs (FiTs), or wheeling arrangements. Recent research shows that around 65 countries implement net-metering to promote rooftop solar, with Pakistan’s evolving policies aiming to incentivize investment and address technical barriers . Smart, bi-directional metering enables precise tracking of energy flows and supports transparent billing and regulatory compliance.

content.title: Tariff Classification & Wheeling Charges
content.body: Wheeling regulations enable third-party electricity delivery across transmission and distribution networks. These rules outline tariff structures, metering boundaries, and responsibilities for energy loss and grid services. For example, Jamaica and Eswatini now have regulatory templates that set clear wheeling methodologies, facilitating greater corporate and industrial uptake of on-site renewables . Transparent wheeling frameworks help balance utility revenue models with fair cost allocation and access to distributed generation.
